subjects.name: Computer Science HL
assessmentObjectives: AO3: Constructing, analysing, evaluating and formulating
AO4: Using skills for effective problem-solving

topics.title: System fundamentals
topics.syllabusDescription: Basic concepts and issues related to the planning, development and maintenance of computer systems.

subtopics.title: Planning and system development
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify the context for which a new system is planned. Describe the need for system change. Outline compatibility, usability and security considerations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Includes legacy systems, business mergers, and factors leading to the need for new systems such as organizational growth or regulatory change.
coreConcepts: New systems arise from changing organizational needs or limitations of existing systems
Different stakeholders may have conflicting requirements
Legacy systems can constrain the design of new systems
Planning must consider hardware, software, data, processes and people
Poorly managed change can lead to system failure or user resistance
commonMisconceptions: Assuming technical requirements are the only important factors
Ignoring user training and documentation in planning
Thinking replacing a system is purely a technical decision
Underestimating the risks of large-scale system changes

conceptual: Explain why involving end-users early in system planning is important.
Describe two reasons why an organization might choose to replace a legacy system.
examStyle: A school is planning to replace its student information system. Identify two stakeholders and describe one possible requirement for each stakeholder. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: System installation and data migration
subtopics.syllabusContent: Methods of system installation and data migration, including direct changeover, parallel running, pilot running and phased implementation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of each method in different organizational contexts.
coreConcepts: System installation methods balance cost, risk and complexity
Direct changeover is fast but high risk if problems occur
Parallel running is safer but more expensive and resource-intensive
Pilot and phased implementations limit risk by restricting scope
Data migration requires validation and testing to avoid data loss or corruption
commonMisconceptions: Assuming direct changeover is always best because it is quickest
Underestimating the time needed for parallel or phased approaches
Thinking migration is just copying files without validation
Ignoring backup strategies during migration

conceptual: Explain why an organization might choose parallel running instead of direct changeover.
Describe one risk associated with data migration and how it can be reduced.
examStyle: Compare direct changeover and parallel running as methods for installing a new hospital information system. [6 marks]

topics.title: Computer organization
topics.syllabusDescription: Structure and function of computer hardware and low-level software.

subtopics.title: Hardware and primary memory
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify the main components of the von Neumann architecture and describe the roles of RAM and ROM.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Include CPU, ALU, control unit, registers, buses, and memory hierarchy at an overview level.
coreConcepts: The CPU executes instructions using the fetch–decode–execute cycle
RAM is volatile memory that stores data and instructions currently in use
ROM is non-volatile and used to store firmware such as the bootstrap program
Buses transfer data, addresses and control signals between components
Overall system performance depends on coordination between CPU and memory
commonMisconceptions: Confusing RAM and secondary storage such as hard drives
Thinking ROM cannot be updated under any circumstances
Assuming CPU speed alone determines overall performance
Using the term 'memory' for any type of storage without distinction

conceptual: Explain the difference between RAM and ROM in terms of volatility and typical use.
Describe the function of the control unit in the CPU.
examStyle: Outline the steps in the fetch–decode–execute cycle. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Secondary storage and input/output
subtopics.syllabusContent: Different types of secondary storage and input/output devices and their characteristics.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Include optical, magnetic and solid-state storage; typical use cases and trade-offs between speed, capacity, and cost.
coreConcepts: Secondary storage is non-volatile and used for long-term data storage
Magnetic, optical and solid-state media differ in speed, durability and cost
Choice of storage depends on capacity, speed, portability and reliability requirements
Input/output devices interface between users and the system
Performance bottlenecks often arise from storage and I/O limitations
commonMisconceptions: Assuming SSDs are always better than HDDs in every respect
Confusing storage capacity with memory size
Ignoring reliability and write endurance when choosing storage
Treating all I/O devices as interchangeable

conceptual: Compare solid-state drives and magnetic hard drives in terms of speed, durability and cost.
Explain why an organization might choose tape backup even when faster storage is available.
examStyle: Describe two factors that influence the choice of secondary storage for a portable media player. [4 marks]

topics.title: Number and algebra
topics.syllabusDescription: This topic develops number skills, algebraic manipulation, and foundational results needed for further study in mathematics.

subtopics.title: Scientific notation and estimation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Scientific notation (standard form) for expressing very large and very small numbers. Use of appropriate accuracy, significant figures, and estimation in calculations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Standard form a × 10^k where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and k ∈ ℤ. Use of significant figures in answers and intermediate steps. Order-of-magnitude estimates in context.
coreConcepts: Scientific notation (standard form) writes numbers as a × 10^k with 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and integer k
Significant figures measure the precision of a number and guide rounding in answers
Order-of-magnitude estimates use powers of 10 to approximate size
Rounding must be consistent with the context and given data accuracy
Small and large physical quantities are conveniently compared using powers of 10
commonMisconceptions: Writing the coefficient a outside the range 1 ≤ |a| < 10
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Rounding too early in multi-step calculations and losing accuracy
Incorrectly handling negative powers of 10 for small numbers
Dropping units when estimating or rounding

conceptual: Explain the difference between significant figures and decimal places in a measurement.
Describe why scientific notation is useful when comparing the sizes of astronomical and subatomic quantities.
examStyle: Write 0.000 045 3 in the form a × 10^k, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and k ∈ ℤ. [2 marks]
The population of a country is 3.2 × 10^8. Estimate the total number of people in 5 such countries, giving your answer to 2 significant figures. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Arithmetic sequences and series
subtopics.syllabusContent: Arithmetic sequences and series. Use of the formulae for the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Use of sigma notation for sums of arithmetic sequences. Students should be familiar with the term “common difference” (d).
coreConcepts: An arithmetic sequence has a constant common difference d between consecutive terms
The nth term formula: un = u1 + (n − 1)d
The sum of the first n terms: Sn = n/2 [2u1 + (n − 1)d]
Alternative sum formula: Sn = n/2 (u1 + un)
Sigma notation compactly represents the sum of sequence terms
commonMisconceptions: Using un = u1 + nd instead of u1 + (n − 1)d
Confusing arithmetic sequences with geometric sequences
Forgetting that (n − 1) represents the number of steps from the first term
Mixing up the two sum formulae when different information is given

conceptual: Explain why the nth term formula contains (n − 1)d rather than nd.
Describe how the sum formula Sn = n/2 (u1 + un) is related to the concept of averaging.
examStyle: The third term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the seventh term is 23. Find the first term and the common difference. [4 marks]
An arithmetic series has first term 5 and common difference 3. Find the smallest value of n for which the sum exceeds 500. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Geometric sequences and series
subtopics.syllabusContent: Geometric sequences and series. Use of the formulae for the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Use of sigma notation for sums of geometric sequences. The sum to infinity of a convergent geometric sequence. Students should be familiar with the term “common ratio” (r).
coreConcepts: A geometric sequence has a constant common ratio r between consecutive terms
The nth term formula: un = u1 × r^(n − 1)
The sum of the first n terms: Sn = u1 (1 − r^n) / (1 − r) for r ≠ 1
For |r| < 1, the sum to infinity: S∞ = u1 / (1 − r)
A geometric series converges only when |r| < 1
commonMisconceptions: Using un = u1 × r^n instead of r^(n − 1)
Confusing geometric and arithmetic sequences
Ignoring the convergence condition |r| < 1 for infinite sums
Applying the sum-to-infinity formula when |r| ≥ 1
Mishandling negative common ratios

conceptual: Explain why the sum to infinity of a geometric series only exists when |r| < 1.
Compare the growth of arithmetic and geometric sequences using an example.
examStyle: A geometric sequence has u1 = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms. [5 marks]
The sum to infinity of a geometric series is 12 and the first term is 4. Find the common ratio. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Sigma notation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Sigma notation. Analysis of arithmetic and geometric series using sigma notation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Including applications in compound interest and population growth. Use of technology to calculate series.
coreConcepts: Sigma notation Σ represents the sum of a sequence of terms
The expression Σ(i = a to b) f(i) means add f(i) from i = a to i = b
The index is a dummy variable that can be renamed without changing the sum
Linear properties: Σ(a + b) = Σa + Σb and Σ(k a) = k Σa for constant k
Sigma notation can represent both arithmetic and geometric series
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the index variable with the terms themselves
Incorrectly using or swapping upper and lower limits
Forgetting to substitute the index correctly into the general term
Misapplying summation properties when expressions are not like terms
Treating the index as a fixed value instead of varying through the sum

conceptual: Explain what the index i represents in Σ(i = 1 to n) ai and why changing i to k does not change the sum.
Describe how sigma notation simplifies the representation of long series.
examStyle: Express the sum 2 + 5 + 8 + 11 + … + 32 using sigma notation. [3 marks]
Evaluate Σ(k = 1 to 10) (3k − 1). [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Financial applications of geometric sequences
subtopics.syllabusContent: Financial applications of geometric sequences and series: compound interest, annual depreciation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Calculate the real value of an investment with an interest rate and an inflation rate. Compound interest may be calculated yearly, half-yearly, quarterly or monthly. Students are not required to derive the formulas.
coreConcepts: Compound interest follows a geometric sequence with ratio (1 + r/n) for n compounding periods per year
Compound interest formula: A = P (1 + r/n)^(nt)
Depreciation can be modelled by V = V0 (1 − r)^t
Real value of money accounts for inflation over time
Different compounding frequencies change the effective growth rate
commonMisconceptions: Confusing compound interest with simple interest
Using yearly interest rate directly for monthly or quarterly compounding
Not converting percentages to decimals in formulas
Ignoring inflation when a question asks for real value
Using the wrong sign of r for appreciation vs depreciation

conceptual: Explain why more frequent compounding (for example monthly instead of yearly) yields a higher final amount.
Describe how geometric growth models both compound interest and inflation.
examStyle: €5000 is invested at 4% per annum compounded yearly. Calculate its value after 6 years. [4 marks]
A machine costing $25 000 depreciates at 15% per annum. Find its value after 5 years. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Laws of exponents and logarithms (basic)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Laws of exponents with integer exponents. Introduction to logarithms with base 10 and base e. Numerical evaluation of logarithms using technology.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Awareness that a^x = b is equivalent to log_a(b) = x, that b > 0, and that log_e(x) is written ln x.
coreConcepts: Integer exponent laws: a^m × a^n = a^(m + n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m − n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn)
a^x = b is equivalent to log_a(b) = x with b > 0 and a > 0, a ≠ 1
The natural logarithm ln x is log_e x where e is an important mathematical constant
Common logarithm log x usually means log_10 x
Logarithms are only defined for positive real arguments
commonMisconceptions: Writing a^m + a^n = a^(m + n) instead of a^m × a^n
Confusing log and ln or treating them as interchangeable bases
Trying to take logarithms of zero or negative numbers
Forgetting that log_a(1) = 0 and log_a(a) = 1
Misidentifying which number is the base in log_a(b)

conceptual: Explain why log_a(1) = 0 for any valid base a.
Describe the relationship between exponential form a^x = b and logarithmic form log_a(b) = x.
examStyle: Write 2^5 = 32 in logarithmic form. [2 marks]
Calculate log_10(1000) without using technology. [2 marks]

subtopics.title: Proof (simple deductive)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Simple deductive proof, numerical and algebraic. Layout of left-hand-side (LHS) to right-hand-side (RHS) proofs. Symbols and notation for equality and identity.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to set out a clear sequence of algebraic steps transforming one side of an identity into the other, and know how to check results.
coreConcepts: A mathematical proof is a logical argument demonstrating that a statement is always true
In LHS = RHS proofs, work from one side to transform it into the other using valid steps
Each algebraic step must follow from previous ones using known rules
The identity symbol (≡) indicates the statement is true for all allowed values
An equation with = may hold only for specific solutions
commonMisconceptions: Working on both sides at the same time in an identity proof
Assuming what must be proved and using it as a step
Skipping logical steps or not showing sufficient working
Confusing equality (=) with identity (≡)
Failing to verify a result with substitution

conceptual: Explain the difference between an identity and an equation with specific solutions.
Describe why each step in an algebraic proof must be justified.
examStyle: Show that (x + 3)^2 − 5 ≡ x^2 + 6x + 4. [3 marks]
Verify that x = 2 is a solution of the equation x^3 − 3x^2 − 4x + 12 = 0. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Laws of exponents and logarithms (extended)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Laws of exponents with rational exponents. Laws of logarithms. Change of base of a logarithm. Solving exponential equations, including using logarithms.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should know that a^(1/m) = mth root of a (positive root for even m). Laws include log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y, log_a(x/y) = log_a x − log_a y, log_a(x^m) = m log_a x, log_a(a) = 1, log_a(1) = 0, and change of base log_a x = log_b x / log_b a.
coreConcepts: Rational exponents: a^(m/n) = (n√a)^m = n√(a^m) for a > 0
Product rule: log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y
Quotient rule: log_a(x/y) = log_a x − log_a y
Power rule: log_a(x^m) = m log_a x
Change of base: log_a x = ln x / ln a or log_b x / log_b a
commonMisconceptions: Writing log(x + y) = log x + log y instead of log(xy)
Assuming log(x − y) = log x − log y
Misapplying the power rule to (log x)^m instead of log(x^m)
Failing to take logarithms of both sides consistently when solving exponential equations
Using negative or zero bases in expressions with rational exponents

conceptual: Explain, using an example, why log_a(x + y) is not equal to log_a x + log_a y.
Describe how the change of base formula allows any logarithm to be evaluated on a calculator.
examStyle: Solve 2^x = 10, giving your answer correct to three significant figures. [4 marks]
Show that log_2(125) = 3 log_2 5. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
subtopics.syllabusContent: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences. Use of the condition |r| < 1 and modulus notation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should recognize when an infinite geometric series converges and apply S∞ = u1 / (1 − r) when |r| < 1.
coreConcepts: An infinite geometric series converges only when |r| < 1
For a convergent geometric series, S∞ = u1 / (1 − r)
When |r| ≥ 1, the series diverges and has no finite sum
The modulus |r| denotes the absolute value of r
If |r| < 1, then r^n → 0 as n → ∞, which underpins the sum formula
commonMisconceptions: Using the sum-to-infinity formula when |r| ≥ 1
Ignoring negative ratios that still satisfy |r| < 1
Confusing the condition |r| < 1 with r < 1 only
Using the finite sum formula Sn instead of the infinite sum formula S∞
Not recognizing that some series given in context are geometric

conceptual: Explain why an infinite geometric series with |r| ≥ 1 cannot have a finite sum.
Describe what happens to the terms of a geometric sequence when |r| < 1.
examStyle: Find the sum to infinity of the series 12 + 6 + 3 + 1.5 + … . [4 marks]
A geometric series has first term 8 and sum to infinity 32. Find the common ratio r. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Permutations and combinations
subtopics.syllabusContent: Permutations and combinations. Use of nPr and nCr in counting and probability problems.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Factorial notation n!. Distinguish between ordered and unordered selections. Simple applications to probability.
coreConcepts: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1 for positive integers n
Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections
Number of r-permutations: nPr = n! / (n − r)!
Number of r-combinations: nCr = n! / (r! (n − r)!)
Permutations and combinations underpin many probability models
commonMisconceptions: Using nCr when the order of objects matters
Using nPr when the order is irrelevant
Including 0 in factorial products incorrectly
Confusing nCr with rCn
Assuming nPr = nCr

conceptual: Explain the difference between permutations and combinations using a concrete example.
Describe why nCr = nC(n − r) using a combinatorial argument.
examStyle: How many different 5-digit codes can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 if no digit is repeated? [4 marks]
A committee of 3 students is to be chosen from a group of 8. Determine the number of different committees that can be formed. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Partial fractions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Decomposition of rational functions into partial fractions with linear factors in the denominator.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Limited to denominators that factor into distinct or repeated linear factors over ℝ. Use in integration appears later.
coreConcepts: A rational function can often be expressed as a sum of simpler fractions
For distinct linear factors, write A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) etc.
Equating coefficients or substituting suitable x-values determines the constants
For repeated linear factors, include terms like A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)^2
Partial fractions simplify later calculus and integration problems
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to include terms for repeated factors
Incorrect expansion when equating coefficients
Cancelling factors before decomposing when it is not appropriate
Mixing up constants between different terms

conceptual: Explain why writing a rational function as a sum of partial fractions can make integration easier.
Describe when repeated linear factors must be used in a partial fraction decomposition.
examStyle: Express (5x + 3) / (x^2 − x − 2) in partial fractions. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Complex numbers (algebraic form)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Introduction to complex numbers in the form a + bi. Real and imaginary parts. Complex conjugate. Modulus and argument (informal).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and representation in the Argand diagram. Quadratic equations with complex roots.
coreConcepts: The imaginary unit i satisfies i^2 = −1
Any complex number can be written as a + bi with a, b ∈ ℝ
Conjugate of a + bi is a − bi; conjugates are symmetric about the real axis
Modulus |z| represents distance from the origin in the Argand plane
Non-real roots of polynomials occur in conjugate pairs when coefficients are real
commonMisconceptions: Treating i as an unknown variable instead of a defined number
Forgetting that i^2 = −1 and hence i^4 = 1, etc.
Incorrectly adding or multiplying complex numbers (mixing real and imaginary parts)
Thinking complex roots contradict the equation having real coefficients

conceptual: Explain why complex roots of a quadratic with real coefficients must occur in conjugate pairs.
Describe how a complex number can be represented as a point in the Argand diagram.
examStyle: Solve the equation x^2 + 4x + 13 = 0, giving your answers in the form a + bi. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Complex numbers (polar form)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Polar (modulus–argument) form of complex numbers. Multiplication and division in polar form.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Use z = r (cos θ + i sin θ). Simple applications of De Moivre’s theorem for integer powers and roots.
coreConcepts: Any non-zero complex number can be written as z = r (cos θ + i sin θ)
r = |z| and θ is an argument of z
Multiplication and division correspond to adding and subtracting arguments, multiplying and dividing moduli
De Moivre’s theorem: [r (cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n (cos nθ + i sin nθ) for integer n
Polar form simplifies powers and roots of complex numbers
commonMisconceptions: Using degrees and radians inconsistently for θ
Ignoring the periodicity of arguments when finding all solutions
Forgetting to multiply the modulus as well as the argument in powers
Confusing argument with modulus

conceptual: Explain why multiplying two complex numbers in polar form corresponds to adding their arguments.
Describe how De Moivre’s theorem can be used to find multiple roots of a complex number.
examStyle: Express z = 1 − i in the form r (cos θ + i sin θ). Hence find z^5 in the same form. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Polynomial equations and complex roots
subtopics.syllabusContent: Fundamental theorem of algebra (informal). Relationship between polynomial coefficients and sums/products of roots. Conjugate root theorem.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Focus on real-coefficient polynomials and simple applications linking roots and coefficients.
coreConcepts: A polynomial of degree n has n complex roots, counting multiplicity
If coefficients are real and a + bi is a root, then a − bi is also a root
For quadratics ax^2 + bx + c, sum of roots = −b/a and product = c/a
Similar relationships exist for higher-degree polynomials
Root–coefficient relationships help in constructing or factoring polynomials
commonMisconceptions: Thinking non-real roots occur alone for real-coefficient polynomials
Misapplying sum/product formulas to polynomials not in standard form
Confusing multiplicity of roots with distinct roots
Assuming all polynomials factor nicely over the reals

conceptual: Explain why a cubic polynomial with real coefficients and one non-real root must have exactly one other non-real root.
Describe how the sum and product of roots are related to the coefficients of a quadratic.
examStyle: The quadratic equation x^2 − 4x + k = 0 has roots 2 ± i. Find the value of k. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Proof by mathematical induction
subtopics.syllabusContent: Simple proofs by mathematical induction for statements involving positive integers.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Restricted to standard forms: sums of series, divisibility, and simple inequalities. Students should clearly identify base case and inductive step.
coreConcepts: Induction proves a statement is true for all integers n ≥ n0
Base case verifies the statement for the initial integer n0
Inductive step assumes truth for n = k and proves it for n = k + 1
Induction relies on the well-ordering of the positive integers
Many identities and divisibility results can be shown using induction
commonMisconceptions: Treating the inductive hypothesis as something to prove rather than assume
Failing to complete the step from n = k to n = k + 1
Not checking the base case explicitly
Using circular reasoning (assuming the result for all n instead of just k)

conceptual: Explain why proving a statement for n = 1 and then proving that if it holds for n = k it holds for n = k + 1 shows it is true for all n ≥ 1.
Describe a situation outside mathematics where a similar inductive idea applies.
examStyle: Prove by mathematical induction that 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 for all positive integers n. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Systems of linear equations
subtopics.syllabusContent: Solution of systems of linear equations in two or three unknowns using algebraic methods and technology. Conditions for unique, no, or infinitely many solutions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Link to matrix methods is made later in the course. Graphical interpretation in 2D and 3D.
coreConcepts: A system of linear equations may have one, none, or infinitely many solutions
In two variables, equations represent lines; the solution corresponds to intersection points
In three variables, equations represent planes and may intersect in a point, line, or not at all
Algebraic elimination and substitution are standard solution methods
Coefficient relationships indicate the nature of the solution set
commonMisconceptions: Assuming every system has a unique solution
Arithmetic mistakes in elimination leading to incorrect conclusions
Confusing inconsistent systems with those having infinite solutions
Not recognizing multiples of equations

conceptual: Explain how you can tell from a pair of linear equations whether there will be no solution, one solution, or infinitely many solutions.
Describe the geometric meaning of a system of three linear equations in three unknowns.
examStyle: Solve the system 2x + 3y − z = 1, x − y + 2z = 4, 3x + 2y + z = 7. [6 marks]

topics.title: Functions
topics.syllabusDescription: This topic develops understanding of functions as mathematical models and explores their algebraic and graphical representations.

subtopics.title: Straight lines
subtopics.syllabusContent: Different forms of the equation of a straight line. Gradient and intercepts. Parallel and perpendicular lines.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Forms include y = mx + c, ax + by + d = 0, and point–gradient form y − y1 = m(x − x1). Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines satisfy m1 m2 = −1.
coreConcepts: Gradient m represents the rate of change of y with respect to x
The y-intercept is the point where the line crosses the y-axis (x = 0)
Parallel lines have equal gradients
Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1
Different algebraic forms can represent the same line
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up x and y when computing gradient
Thinking perpendicular gradients add to zero instead of multiplying to −1
Forgetting that vertical lines have undefined gradient
Errors when rearranging between different line forms
Assuming any two distinct lines are either parallel or perpendicular

conceptual: Explain why parallel lines must have the same gradient.
Describe algebraically the relationship between the gradients of perpendicular lines.
examStyle: Find the equation of the line passing through (2, 5) with gradient 3. [3 marks]
Show that the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = −0.5x + 4 are perpendicular. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Concept of a function
subtopics.syllabusContent: Concept of a function, domain, range and graph. Function notation f(x), v(t), C(n). Inverse function as reflection in y = x, notation f⁻¹(x).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Informal idea that an inverse function “undoes” a function. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions. The domain of f⁻¹ equals the range of f.
coreConcepts: A function assigns each element of its domain exactly one image in its range
Domain is the set of allowable input values for the function
Range is the set of actual output values
An inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function
The graph of an inverse function is a reflection of the original graph in the line y = x
commonMisconceptions: Confusing f⁻¹(x) with 1 / f(x)
Assuming every function has an inverse
Confusing the range with the codomain
Ignoring domain restrictions when defining an inverse
Misusing the vertical line test and horizontal line test

conceptual: Explain why f(x) = x^2 does not have an inverse function on ℝ unless its domain is restricted.
Describe graphically the relationship between a function and its inverse.
examStyle: For f(x) = 2x − 3, find f⁻¹(x). [3 marks]
State the domain and range of f(x) = √(x − 2). [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Graphing functions
subtopics.syllabusContent: The graph of a function y = f(x). Sketching graphs from information given or context. Using technology to graph functions, including sums and differences.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should distinguish between “sketch” and “draw”. Axes and key features must be labelled. Functions not explicitly listed in the syllabus may appear in graphs.
coreConcepts: A sketch shows the general shape and key features without precise scale
A drawn graph is plotted accurately using a scale
Key features include intercepts, turning points, asymptotes and end behavior
Technology helps visualize complicated functions and combinations
The graph of (f + g)(x) is obtained by adding function values f(x) + g(x)
commonMisconceptions: Not labelling axes or important points
Ignoring instructions to sketch versus draw
Missing asymptotes, intercepts, or other key features
Incorrectly estimating the shape between plotted points
Using an inappropriate or inconsistent scale

conceptual: Explain the difference between sketching a graph and drawing a graph.
Describe which features must always appear on a sketch of a function.
examStyle: Sketch the graph of f(x) = x^2 − 4, indicating all intercepts. [3 marks]
Use technology to graph f(x) = e^x and g(x) = ln x on the same set of axes and comment on their relationship. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Key features of graphs
subtopics.syllabusContent: Determining key features of graphs: maximum and minimum values, intercepts, symmetry, vertex, zeros/roots, vertical and horizontal asymptotes, and intersections.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Technology may be needed to find features for complicated functions. Students should interpret these features in context where appropriate.
coreConcepts: Zeros or roots correspond to x-intercepts where f(x) = 0
A local maximum (minimum) is the highest (lowest) point in a neighbourhood
Vertical asymptotes arise where the function grows without bound near certain x-values
Horizontal asymptotes describe the limiting value of a function as x → ±∞
Symmetry (even/odd) can be recognized graphically and algebraically
commonMisconceptions: Confusing local extrema with global extrema
Believing a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote
Treating the y-intercept as a root of the function
Missing multiple roots or repeated roots
Confusing the vertex of a quadratic with any point of symmetry

conceptual: Explain the difference between a local maximum and an absolute maximum.
Describe what a horizontal asymptote tells you about the long-term behaviour of a function.
examStyle: Find the coordinates of the vertex of f(x) = 2(x − 3)^2 + 1. [2 marks]
Using technology, find all points of intersection of f(x) = x^3 − 2x and g(x) = x + 1. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Composite and inverse functions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Composite functions f ∘ g(x) = f(g(x)). Identity function. Finding inverse functions f⁻¹(x). Existence of inverses for one-to-one functions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand that f ∘ f⁻¹(x) = f⁻¹ ∘ f(x) = x on appropriate domains. Graphical link to reflection in y = x.
coreConcepts: Composite function f ∘ g applies g first, then f to the result
Composition is generally not commutative: f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f
The identity function I(x) = x leaves values unchanged
An inverse reverses the effect of a function, satisfying f(f⁻¹(x)) = x where defined
Only one-to-one functions admit global inverses over their domains
commonMisconceptions: Treating f ∘ g as multiplication of functions rather than composition
Reversing the order: thinking f ∘ g(x) = g(f(x))
Ignoring domain and range when defining inverses
Assuming every function has an inverse function
Confusing f⁻¹(x) with [f(x)]⁻¹

conceptual: Explain why f ∘ g is usually not equal to g ∘ f.
Describe what it means for a function to be one-to-one and why this matters for inverses.
examStyle: Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, find f ∘ g(x) and g ∘ f(x). [4 marks]
Find the inverse function of f(x) = (x − 3)/2, stating its domain. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Quadratic functions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Quadratic function f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c and its graph. Standard, factored, and vertex forms.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Forms: f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, f(x) = a(x − p)(x − q), f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k. Students should convert between forms and relate them to graph features.
coreConcepts: Standard form shows the y-intercept at (0, c)
Factored form reveals real roots and x-intercepts (if they exist)
Vertex form gives the vertex (h, k) directly
Axis of symmetry is x = h or x = −b/(2a)
The sign of a determines whether the parabola opens upwards or downwards
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the vertex is always at the origin
Sign errors when completing the square or converting forms
Confusing h with −h in vertex form
Expecting factored form even when roots are complex
Misidentifying the axis of symmetry

conceptual: Explain why the vertex form immediately shows the maximum or minimum value of a quadratic.
Describe how the parameter a affects the shape and width of the parabola.
examStyle: Express f(x) = x^2 + 6x + 5 in the form f(x) = (x − h)^2 + k. [3 marks]
A quadratic function has vertex (2, −3) and passes through (0, 5). Find its equation. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Solving quadratic equations
subtopics.syllabusContent: Solution of quadratic equations and inequalities. Quadratic formula and discriminant Δ = b^2 − 4ac and the nature of roots.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Methods include factorization, completing the square, and the quadratic formula. Discriminant: Δ > 0 two distinct real roots, Δ = 0 one repeated real root, Δ < 0 no real roots.
coreConcepts: Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a)
The discriminant Δ = b^2 − 4ac determines the nature of the roots
Δ > 0 gives two distinct real roots (the graph cuts the x-axis twice)
Δ = 0 gives one repeated real root (the graph touches the x-axis)
Δ < 0 gives no real roots (the graph does not intersect the x-axis)
commonMisconceptions: Sign errors, particularly with −b in the quadratic formula
Forgetting the ± sign and obtaining only one root
Dividing only part of the numerator by 2a
Misinterpreting Δ ≥ 0 vs Δ > 0
Leaving surds unsimplified in exact answers

conceptual: Explain how the discriminant indicates the number of x-intercepts of the quadratic function.
Describe the graphical meaning of a repeated root.
examStyle: Solve x^2 − 5x + 6 = 0. [3 marks]
Find the values of k for which kx^2 + 4x + k = 0 has two distinct real roots. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Rational functions (SL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Simple rational functions of the form f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d) and their graphs. Vertical and horizontal asymptotes, holes not required at SL.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should identify asymptotes and intercepts and sketch graphs. Use technology where algebraic analysis is difficult.
coreConcepts: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the function is undefined
Horizontal asymptotes give the end behaviour as x → ±∞
Intercepts are found by setting x or y equal to zero
Transformations can shift and stretch the basic 1/x graph
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a function can never cross a horizontal asymptote
Forgetting to exclude points where the denominator is zero
Confusing vertical asymptotes with x-intercepts
Incorrectly drawing the branches of the graph in wrong quadrants
Assuming all rational functions look like 1/x

conceptual: Explain the difference between vertical and horizontal asymptotes for a rational function.
Describe how the graph of y = 1/x changes when it is transformed to y = 2/(x − 3) + 1.
examStyle: Sketch the graph of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 1), showing all asymptotes and intercepts. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Exponential functions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Functions of the form f(x) = a^x and their graphs, for a > 0, a ≠ 1. Applications to growth and decay.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Emphasis on shape of graphs, intercepts, and asymptotes. Link to logarithmic functions as inverses.
coreConcepts: For a > 1, f(x) = a^x models exponential growth; for 0 < a < 1, exponential decay
The graph passes through (0, 1) and has y = 0 as a horizontal asymptote
The base a controls the rate of growth or decay
Exponential functions are one-to-one and have inverses
Many real-life processes can be approximated by exponential models
commonMisconceptions: Confusing linear and exponential growth in word problems
Thinking a^0 = 0 instead of 1
Drawing the graph crossing the x-axis
Using negative bases for real-valued exponential functions
Not recognizing decay when 0 < a < 1

conceptual: Explain why an exponential function with base greater than 1 always increases.
Describe how the graph of y = 3^x differs from the graph of y = 2^x.
examStyle: Sketch the graph of f(x) = 2^x, indicating the intercept with the y-axis and any asymptotes. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Solving equations graphically and with technology
subtopics.syllabusContent: Solving equations of the form f(x) = g(x) using graphs and technology. Intersection points of curves.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should interpret intersections in context. Technology may be required when algebraic solutions are difficult or impossible.
coreConcepts: Solutions of f(x) = g(x) correspond to intersection points of their graphs
Graphical methods provide approximate solutions
Technology can be used to find numerical solutions to complicated equations
Different equations can have zero, one, or several real solutions
Approximate solutions should be rounded appropriately and checked
commonMisconceptions: Reading off approximate solutions too coarsely from a graph
Forgetting that equations can have no real solutions
Misinterpreting multiple intersections as a single solution
Not verifying solutions by substitution
Over-reliance on technology without understanding the graphs

conceptual: Explain why some equations can be solved algebraically while others require numerical or graphical methods.
Describe how you would use a graphing calculator to solve f(x) = g(x).
examStyle: Use technology to solve the equation e^x = x + 2, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Transformations of graphs
subtopics.syllabusContent: Graphical effects of transformations of the form y = f(x) + a, y = f(x − a), y = k f(x), y = f(kx).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should link algebraic changes in the function expression to vertical and horizontal shifts and stretches. Reflections may also be included.
coreConcepts: y = f(x) + a translates the graph vertically by a units
y = f(x − a) translates the graph horizontally by a units
y = k f(x) scales the graph vertically by factor k
y = f(kx) scales the graph horizontally by factor 1/k
Reflections such as y = −f(x) and y = f(−x) flip the graph in the axes
commonMisconceptions: Confusing inside and outside changes (x − a vs + a) in the function
Reversing the direction of horizontal translations
Misinterpreting horizontal stretches as vertical ones
Forgetting that horizontal scaling uses reciprocal factors
Applying transformations in the wrong order when multiple changes occur

conceptual: Explain how the graph of y = (x − 2)^2 + 3 is obtained from the graph of y = x^2.
Describe the effect on the graph of f of changing f(x) to −f(x) and to f(−x).
examStyle: The graph of y = f(x) is shown. Sketch the graphs of y = f(x − 2) and y = 2f(x) on the same axes. [4 marks]

topics.title: Geometry and trigonometry
topics.syllabusDescription: This topic develops geometrical reasoning, trigonometric skills, and spatial visualization, including mensuration, trigonometric functions and identities, equations, and vectors in two and three dimensions for modeling and problem-solving.

subtopics.title: Mensuration in two and three dimensions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Perimeter, area and volume for standard plane and solid figures, including rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, circles, prisms, pyramids, cones and spheres. Use of composite shapes and solids in problem-solving.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Formulae for basic 2D and 3D figures are provided in the formula booklet. Problems may involve combining several shapes, interpreting diagrams, and working with exact values and approximations. Units and unit conversions should be emphasized.
coreConcepts: Area and volume formulae model real measurements of two- and three-dimensional objects
Decomposing complex shapes into simpler standard shapes simplifies area and volume calculations
Consistency of units is essential when calculating and interpreting measurements
Scaling linear dimensions affects area and volume by square and cube factors respectively
Many real-life applications, such as packaging and construction, rely on geometric measurement
commonMisconceptions: Using diameter instead of radius in circle formulae
Confusing surface area with volume in word problems
Forgetting to convert all lengths to the same units before calculation
Assuming a direct linear relationship between changes in length and changes in area or volume
Omitting hidden or interior faces when computing surface area of composite solids

conceptual: Explain how doubling the dimensions of a cube affects its surface area and its volume.
Describe a strategy for finding the volume of a composite solid made of a cylinder and a cone.
examStyle: A solid is composed of a right circular cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 10 cm, with a hemisphere of the same radius attached to one end. Calculate the total volume of the solid, giving your answer to three significant figures. [6 marks]

The base of a triangular prism is a right triangle with legs 5 cm and 12 cm. The length of the prism is 20 cm. Find the total surface area of the prism, excluding the base that rests on the ground. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Sine rule, cosine rule and area of a triangle
subtopics.syllabusContent: Sine rule, cosine rule, and area of a triangle ½ab sin C for any triangle. Use of these results in solving triangles, including applications in two and three dimensions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The sine rule should be applied in the forms a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C and sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c. The cosine rule may be used to find unknown sides or angles. Questions can involve bearings, angles of elevation and depression, and non-right-angled contexts.
coreConcepts: The sine and cosine rules generalize Pythagoras' theorem to any triangle
The formula area = ½ab sin C allows areas of non-right-angled triangles to be found using two sides and the included angle
Trigonometric rules connect geometric measurements in navigation, surveying and physics
Choosing the appropriate rule depends on the known combination of sides and angles
The sine rule can yield the ambiguous case when solving for angles
commonMisconceptions: Applying the sine rule when the cosine rule is required and vice versa
Using the wrong angle in the area formula ½ab sin C (not the included angle)
Ignoring the possibility of two solutions for an angle when using the sine rule
Confusing side labels with angle labels in the sine and cosine rules
Rounding intermediate values too early and causing inaccuracy in final answers

conceptual: Explain when the sine rule leads to an ambiguous case and how this affects the solution of a triangle.
Describe how the cosine rule can be viewed as a generalization of Pythagoras' theorem.
examStyle: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 7.6 cm, AC = 9.1 cm and angle BAC = 58°. Calculate the length of BC and the area of triangle ABC. [6 marks]
From a point P, the bearing of a lighthouse L is 042° and its distance is 12 km. From another point Q, 8 km due east of P, the bearing of the same lighthouse is 316°. Find the distance QL. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Applications of right-angled and non-right-angled trigonometry
subtopics.syllabusContent: Applications of trigonometry to model and solve problems in two and three dimensions, including angles of elevation and depression, navigation, kinematics and resultant forces.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems may involve multiple steps, constructing diagrams from written descriptions, and interpreting solutions in context. Emphasis should be on selecting appropriate trigonometric methods and justifying reasoning.
coreConcepts: Trigonometric ratios and rules model real-world measurements and forces
Constructing accurate diagrams from verbal descriptions is key to solving contextual problems
Many 3D problems can be reduced to linked 2D trigonometric problems
Resolving quantities into perpendicular components often simplifies complex situations
Interpreting results requires attention to units, direction and physical plausibility
commonMisconceptions: Drawing incorrect or incomplete diagrams that do not match the scenario
Mixing up angles of elevation and depression
Assuming all problems can be treated as right triangles when non-right-angled methods are needed
Ignoring directions when combining forces or displacements
Forgetting to convert between degrees and radians when required

conceptual: Explain how resolving a vector into horizontal and vertical components can simplify the analysis of motion on an inclined plane.
Describe how you would model the height of a building using an angle of elevation and a measured horizontal distance.
examStyle: A ship sails 40 km on a bearing of 060° and then 25 km on a bearing of 135°. Find the ship's distance and bearing from its starting point, giving the bearing to the nearest degree. [8 marks]
A ladder of length 4.5 m rests against a vertical wall with its foot 1.2 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground and the height at which it touches the wall. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Radian measure, arc length and area of a sector
subtopics.syllabusContent: Radian measure of angles. Length of an arc and area of a sector of a circle. Relationship between degrees and radians.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Use of formulas s = rθ and A = ½r²θ where θ is in radians. Questions should involve conversion between degrees and radians and may require working with exact forms such as π/3 or 5π/4.
coreConcepts: Radian measure defines angles in terms of arc length relative to radius
There is a constant proportional relationship between degrees and radians
Arc length and sector area are directly proportional to the central angle in radians
Using radians simplifies many trigonometric and calculus relationships
Exact radian measures often lead to exact values of trigonometric functions
commonMisconceptions: Using degree measures directly in formulas that require radians
Confusing arc length and chord length
Incorrectly converting between degrees and radians
Forgetting that 2π radians corresponds to a full revolution
Assuming sector area formulas work with any angle unit without adjustment

conceptual: Explain why radian measure is particularly convenient when working with trigonometric functions in calculus.
Describe how the formula for the area of a sector arises from the ratio of the central angle to 2π.
examStyle: Convert 135° to radians and express your answer in terms of π. [2 marks]
A circle has radius 6 cm. Find the length of the arc and the area of the sector subtended by a central angle of 2.4 radians. Give each answer to three significant figures. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Trigonometric functions and the unit circle
subtopics.syllabusContent: Definition of sine, cosine and tangent for all real numbers using the unit circle. Graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x, including domain, range, amplitude, period, symmetry and key points.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Angles should be considered in radians. Emphasis on periodicity, symmetry (even and odd functions), and connections between the unit circle and graphs. Technology may be used to explore graphs and transformations.
coreConcepts: The unit circle provides a geometric definition of sine and cosine for all real angles
Trigonometric functions are periodic and model repeating phenomena
The graphs of sine, cosine and tangent reflect their definitions on the unit circle
Symmetry properties classify cosine as even and sine and tangent as odd functions
Key features such as amplitude, period and phase shift determine the shape and position of trig graphs
commonMisconceptions: Restricting sine and cosine to acute angles instead of all real angles
Confusing radians and degrees when interpreting graphs
Misidentifying the period of the tangent function compared to sine and cosine
Incorrectly locating zeros and maximum/minimum points
Assuming amplitude applies to the tangent function in the same way as sine and cosine

conceptual: Explain how the unit circle can be used to justify that sin(−x) = −sin x and cos(−x) = cos x.
Describe how the graph of y = sin(x) changes when it is transformed to y = 3 sin(x − π/4).
examStyle: Sketch the graph of y = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, indicating clearly all intercepts and key points where x is a multiple of π/2. [5 marks]
The function f is defined by f(x) = 2 sin(3x) for x ∈ [0, 2π]. State the amplitude and period of f, and sketch its graph on the given axes. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Trigonometric identities
subtopics.syllabusContent: Trigonometric identities including Pythagorean identities, compound angle formulas, double-angle and related identities. Use of identities to simplify expressions and solve equations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be familiar with the identities sin²x + cos²x = 1, 1 + tan²x = sec²x, and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x, as well as compound angle formulae such as sin(A ± B) and cos(A ± B). Proof of standard identities is expected at HL.
coreConcepts: Trigonometric identities express fundamental relationships that hold for all values in their domains
Pythagorean identities derive from the geometry of the unit circle
Compound and double-angle identities allow transformation of trigonometric expressions
Proving identities requires logical manipulation from one side to the other using known relationships
Simplifying expressions using identities often makes equations easier to solve
commonMisconceptions: Treating identities as equations to be solved for specific values of x instead of relationships valid for all x
Attempting to manipulate both sides of an identity simultaneously in an unstructured way
Incorrectly applying or memorizing compound angle formulas
Dividing by expressions that may be zero, thus losing solutions
Confusing identities with conditional equations that hold only for some values

conceptual: Explain why the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1 holds for all real x using the unit circle.
Describe a general strategy you would use to prove a trigonometric identity.
examStyle: Prove the identity sin(2x) = 2 sin x cos x. [4 marks]
Show that 1 + tan²x = sec²x and hence solve the equation sec²x − 5 tan x − 6 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Trigonometric equations
subtopics.syllabusContent: Solution of trigonometric equations in a given interval, including equations that can be reduced to quadratics in sin x, cos x or tan x. Use of trigonometric identities and graphs.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to solve equations of the form a sin x + b cos x = c and those involving multiple angles, using algebraic methods and technology for verification. Solutions should be given within a specified domain, often in radians.
coreConcepts: Trigonometric equations often have multiple solutions within a given interval due to periodicity
Transforming equations to quadratics in a single trig function can simplify solving
Unit circle and graphs help visualize the location of solutions
Restrictions on the domain must be applied carefully when listing solutions
Using identities can reduce complex trig equations to more manageable forms
commonMisconceptions: Giving only one solution where multiple solutions exist
Ignoring the specified interval or mixing degree and radian solutions
Treating sin²x or cos²x as sin x² or cos x² when rearranging equations
Losing solutions when taking square roots or dividing by a trigonometric expression
Failing to check solutions back in the original equation when identities are used

conceptual: Explain why the equation sin x = k can have two solutions between 0 and 2π when −1 < k < 1.
Describe how a trigonometric equation can be transformed into a quadratic equation and why this is useful.
examStyle: Solve the equation 2 sin²x + 3 sin x − 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π. [6 marks]
Solve the equation 3 cos x + 4 sin x = 2 for x ∈ [0, 2π]. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Reciprocal trigonometric functions and further identities (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Reciprocal trigonometric functions sec x, cosec x and cot x. Further identities and properties involving these functions, including relationships with sine, cosine and tangent.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should use the relationships sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x, and understand their domains and ranges. Problems may involve graphing these functions and using identities to simplify expressions.
coreConcepts: Reciprocal trigonometric functions extend the trigonometric toolkit for modeling and analysis
The domains of sec x, cosec x and cot x exclude values where the corresponding base functions are zero
Graphs of reciprocal functions exhibit vertical asymptotes at the zeros of the original functions
Identities with reciprocal functions derive from basic Pythagorean and quotient identities
Understanding domains and asymptotes is crucial when solving equations involving reciprocal functions
commonMisconceptions: Assuming reciprocal trig functions are always defined when sine or cosine is small but non-zero
Ignoring asymptotes and domain restrictions when sketching graphs
Confusing sec x with 1/cos x numerically when cos x is negative
Treating cot x as cos x/sin x without considering domain issues
Mixing degrees and radians when identifying key features on graphs

conceptual: Explain how the graph of y = sec x can be obtained from the graph of y = cos x.
Describe the domain and range of the function y = cot x over one period.
examStyle: Sketch the graph of y = sec x for −π ≤ x ≤ π, indicating all asymptotes and intercepts. [6 marks]
Show that 1 + cot²x = cosec²x and hence simplify the expression (1 + cot²x)/cosec x. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Inverse trigonometric functions (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Definition and principal values of inverse trigonometric functions sin⁻¹x, cos⁻¹x and tan⁻¹x. Graphs and basic properties, including domains and ranges chosen to define inverses.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should know the principal value ranges for inverse trigonometric functions and be able to evaluate simple expressions, sketch graphs and solve equations involving inverse functions. Composition with trigonometric functions should be interpreted carefully.
coreConcepts: Inverse trigonometric functions reverse the effect of trigonometric functions on restricted domains
Principal value ranges are chosen to make trigonometric functions one-to-one and hence invertible
Graphs of inverse trig functions are reflections of the original functions in y = x over restricted domains
Solving equations with inverse trigonometric functions requires attention to principal values and general solutions
Compositions like sin(tan⁻¹x) require interpreting the geometric meaning of the inverse
commonMisconceptions: Assuming inverse trigonometric functions undo trigonometric functions for all angles without restriction
Mixing up degrees and radians when interpreting principal values
Confusing sin⁻¹x with 1/sin x instead of arcsin x
Failing to distinguish between general solutions and principal values in equation solving
Incorrectly reflecting graphs when sketching inverse functions

conceptual: Explain why the domain of y = sin x must be restricted to define an inverse function y = sin⁻¹x.
Describe how to obtain the graph of y = tan⁻¹x from the graph of y = tan x.
examStyle: State the domain and range of the function y = cos⁻¹x. [2 marks]
Solve the equation sin(2x) = ∝ for x ∈ [0, 2π] given that x = sin⁻¹k for some constant k, clearly indicating how you use inverse functions. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Further trigonometric identities and equations (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Further identities, including sum-to-product and product-to-sum forms, and more advanced trigonometric equations involving multiple angles and combinations of functions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems may require using known identities in creative ways, including substitution and algebraic manipulation. Solutions can involve both analytic methods and graphing technology for verification.
coreConcepts: Advanced trigonometric identities extend the ability to transform and simplify complex expressions
Multiple angle equations can often be converted to equations in a single trigonometric function
Choice of substitution plays a key role in solving complicated trig equations
Graphical insight supports and checks algebraic solutions to trigonometric equations
Understanding structure in expressions guides the selection of appropriate identities
commonMisconceptions: Trying to memorize too many identities without understanding how to derive or apply them
Randomly applying identities that do not simplify the expression
Overlooking restrictions on the domain when dividing by trigonometric expressions
Failing to check solutions lost or introduced during algebraic manipulation
Relying only on technology without explaining the underlying reasoning

conceptual: Explain how sum-to-product identities can be helpful in integrating certain trigonometric expressions in calculus.
Describe a situation in which rewriting a trigonometric equation using a substitution simplifies its solution.
examStyle: Show that cos x + cos 3x = 2 cos 2x cos x and hence solve the equation cos x + cos 3x = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π. [8 marks]
Solve the equation 2 sin 2x = 1 + cos 2x for x ∈ [0, 2π]. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Vectors in two and three dimensions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Vectors in two and three dimensions, including representation, magnitude and direction, addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication. Position vectors and displacement.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Vectors may be represented in component form or as directed line segments. Problems include geometric interpretation and applications to displacement and velocity.
coreConcepts: Vectors represent quantities with magnitude and direction in two or three dimensions
Vector addition and scalar multiplication obey geometric and algebraic rules
Position vectors locate points relative to an origin in space
Displacement vectors represent change in position independently of path taken
Vector representations unify geometric, physical and algebraic views of motion
commonMisconceptions: Treating vectors as ordinary numbers without direction
Adding magnitudes instead of components when combining vectors
Confusing displacement with distance travelled
Ignoring signs when interpreting components in coordinate systems
Mixing up position vectors and displacement vectors between points

conceptual: Explain the difference between a position vector and a displacement vector.
Describe how to find the magnitude and direction of the sum of two vectors given in component form.
examStyle: Given the points A(1, 2, −1) and B(4, −0, 3), find the vector AB and its magnitude. [4 marks]
A particle moves from O(0, 0, 0) to P(3, 4, −1) and then to Q(5, 1, 2). Find the displacement vector OQ and its magnitude. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Scalar product and angle between vectors (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Scalar (dot) product of vectors in two and three dimensions. Use to find the angle between vectors and to determine orthogonality.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should use both component and geometric forms of the scalar product and be able to apply these to problems in geometry and physics, such as work done by a force.
coreConcepts: The scalar product combines two vectors to produce a real number encoding angle and magnitude information
Orthogonal vectors have zero scalar product
The scalar product can be expressed using components or magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between vectors
Angles between vectors in space generalize familiar planar angle concepts
Physical quantities such as work can be modeled using the scalar product
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the scalar product with vector multiplication that yields another vector
Incorrectly computing the scalar product by multiplying magnitudes only
Assuming vectors are orthogonal only if their magnitudes are equal
Using degrees when a formula is derived assuming radian measure
Misinterpreting negative scalar products as impossible rather than representing obtuse angles

conceptual: Explain what information about two vectors is captured by their scalar product.
Describe how you can use the scalar product to test whether two vectors are perpendicular.
examStyle: Given vectors a = (2, −1, 3) and b = (1, 4, 2), find a · b and the angle between a and b, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [6 marks]
A constant force F = (5, −2, 1) acts on a particle which moves through a displacement d = (3, 4, 0). Calculate the work done by the force. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Vector equations of lines
subtopics.syllabusContent: Vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions. Parametric representation, points of intersection and relationships between lines (parallel, intersecting, skew).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should write lines in the form r = a + λb and convert between vector and parametric forms. Problems include determining if lines intersect, are parallel or skew, and finding points of intersection when they exist.
coreConcepts: Lines in space can be represented parametrically using a point and a direction vector
Vector and parametric equations offer flexible methods for solving geometrical problems
Relationships between lines can be studied using direction vectors and positions
Intersections are found by equating vector expressions and solving for parameters
Parallel and skew lines can be distinguished using direction vectors and relative positions
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the parameter with a coordinate variable
Assuming lines that are not parallel must intersect in three-dimensional space
Failing to check all components when solving for intersection points
Misinterpreting equal direction vectors as implying the same line rather than parallel lines
Separating vector equations into incorrect parametric component equations

conceptual: Explain how a vector equation of a line encodes both a point on the line and its direction.
Describe how to determine whether two lines in three-dimensional space intersect, are parallel or are skew.
examStyle: A line l passes through the point A(2, −1, 3) and has direction vector d = (1, 4, −2). Write down the vector and parametric equations of l. [4 marks]
Lines l₁ and l₂ have vector equations r = (1, 2, −1) + λ(2, 1, 3) and r = (5, 0, 2) + μ(1, −1, 4). Determine whether the lines intersect, and if so, find their point of intersection. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Vector product and area (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Vector (cross) product of vectors in three dimensions and its use in finding the area of parallelograms and triangles and determining perpendicular vectors.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should compute cross products using components and understand that the result is a vector perpendicular to the original pair. Applications include finding areas and normals to planes.
coreConcepts: The vector product of two non-parallel vectors in space is orthogonal to both
The magnitude of the cross product equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the vectors
The cross product encodes both magnitude and direction information relevant to area and orientation
Normal vectors to planes can be obtained using cross products of direction vectors
Geometric and algebraic interpretations of the cross product are linked through determinants
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the cross product with the scalar product
Forgetting that the cross product is not commutative (a × b ≠ b × a)
Incorrectly computing the sign of components when using determinant methods
Assuming the zero vector cannot arise as a cross product
Mixing up area of a parallelogram and area of a triangle in applications

conceptual: Explain why the cross product of two parallel vectors is the zero vector.
Describe how the vector product can be used to find the area of a triangle in three-dimensional space.
examStyle: Given vectors a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (2, −1, 4), calculate a × b and find the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b. [6 marks]
Points A(1, 0, 2), B(3, 4, 1) and C(2, −1, 5) define a triangle. Use vectors to find the area of triangle ABC. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Lines and planes in three dimensions (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Vector and Cartesian equations of planes. Relationships between lines and planes, including intersection, parallelism and the angle between them.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should work with equations of planes in the forms r = a + λb + μm and n · (r − a) = 0 and convert between vector and Cartesian forms. Problems include finding intersections of lines and planes and distances from points to planes.
coreConcepts: Planes in space can be represented using normal vectors and point-normal forms
Relationships between lines and planes extend two-dimensional geometry to three dimensions
Angles between lines and planes or between planes can be computed using scalar products
Systems of equations arising from vector and Cartesian forms can be solved to find intersections
Distance from a point to a plane has a geometric interpretation in terms of projection
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the direction vector of a line with the normal vector of a plane
Assuming a line is parallel to a plane whenever their equations share some coefficients
Incorrectly computing distances by using non-normal directions
Failing to check if a point lies in a plane when given its equation
Misinterpreting the angle between planes as the angle between their normals

conceptual: Explain how a normal vector defines a plane and how different normal vectors can define the same plane.
Describe how to find the angle between two planes given their Cartesian equations.
examStyle: A plane π has equation 2x − y + 3z = 5. Find a normal vector to π and a point that lies on π, and write a vector equation for the plane. [5 marks]

A line l has vector equation r = (1, 2, 0) + λ(2, −1, 1) and a plane π has equation x + y + z = 4. Determine whether l is parallel to π, lies in π or intersects π, and if it intersects, find the point of intersection. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Further vector geometry (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Applications of vectors to more advanced geometric problems, including shortest distances between skew lines, and geometric loci in three dimensions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems may combine scalar and vector products, parametric equations and plane geometry. Emphasis is on setting up equations using vector methods and interpreting solutions geometrically.
coreConcepts: Vector methods provide powerful tools for solving complex geometric problems in three dimensions
The shortest distance between skew lines can be found using vector products and projections
Geometric loci can often be described succinctly using vector and parametric equations
Combining vector equations of lines and planes yields rich geometric information
Interpreting algebraic results geometrically deepens understanding of spatial relationships
commonMisconceptions: Assuming skew lines must intersect in three dimensions
Using incorrect direction vectors when finding shortest distances
Treating loci in three dimensions as if they were restricted to a plane
Relying only on diagrams without verifying algebraic relationships
Confusing the roles of parameters in describing different loci

conceptual: Explain what is meant by skew lines and how vectors can be used to find the shortest distance between them.
Describe how a locus in three-dimensional space can be represented using a vector equation.
examStyle: Lines l₁ and l₂ have vector equations r = (1, 2, 3) + λ(1, −1, 2) and r = (4, 0, 1) + μ(2, 1, −1). Show that the lines are skew and find the shortest distance between them. [11 marks]
Describe the locus of points P(x, y, z) that satisfy the vector equation r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(0, 1, 1) + μ(1, 1, 0), and explain its geometric meaning. [6 marks]

topics.title: Statistics and probability
topics.syllabusDescription: This topic develops skills in descriptive statistics, probability models, discrete and continuous random variables, and statistical inference, with applications to data analysis, decision-making and uncertainty quantification.

subtopics.title: Presentation of data
subtopics.syllabusContent: Presentation of data in tabular and graphical forms including frequency histograms, box plots, cumulative frequency graphs, and stem-and-leaf diagrams. Use of technology.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should construct and interpret graphical displays, recognize appropriate representations for different data types, and discuss advantages and limitations of each method. Emphasis on reading and interpreting information from graphs.
coreConcepts: Graphical representations reveal patterns, trends and outliers in data distributions
Choice of graph depends on data type, purpose and intended audience
Box plots summarize five-number statistics and facilitate comparisons between distributions
Cumulative frequency graphs enable estimation of medians, quartiles and probabilities
Stem-and-leaf plots preserve original data while showing distribution shape
commonMisconceptions: Confusing bar charts (categorical data) with histograms (continuous data)
Incorrectly calculating quartiles from box plots or cumulative frequency graphs
Ignoring scale and axis labeling when interpreting graphical data
Assuming outliers are always errors rather than potentially significant observations
Misreading cumulative frequency values as ordinary frequencies

conceptual: Explain why a histogram is appropriate for continuous data while a bar chart suits categorical data.
Describe how a box plot summarizes the key features of a data distribution.
examStyle: The following data shows the times (in minutes) taken by 20 students to complete a test: 45, 52, 48, 55, 62, 47, 51, 58, 60, 49, 53, 57, 61, 46, 50, 59, 54, 63, 56, 44. Draw a stem-and-leaf diagram for this data. [3 marks]
A box plot shows the following statistics for test scores: min=42, Q1=58, median=65, Q3=78, max=92. Describe the distribution and identify any outliers if the upper fence is 91. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Measures of central tendency and spread
subtopics.syllabusContent: Mean, median, mode, midrange, range, interquartile range and standard deviation for discrete and continuous data. Use of technology for calculations and interpretations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand the effects of outliers and skewness on measures of central tendency and spread, and select appropriate statistics for different data types and purposes. Emphasis on interpretation in context.
coreConcepts: Different measures of central tendency are sensitive to different aspects of data distributions
Measures of spread quantify the variability and dispersion within datasets
Standard deviation measures typical deviation from the mean and is used in probability
Outliers affect mean and standard deviation more than median and interquartile range
Context determines which summary statistics are most appropriate and interpretable
commonMisconceptions: Using mean for skewed data where median is more representative
Calculating standard deviation incorrectly by squaring deviations before averaging
Confusing population standard deviation with sample standard deviation
Assuming larger standard deviation always means 'worse' or more variable quality
Ignoring units when interpreting measures of spread

conceptual: Explain why the median is preferred over the mean for describing the center of a highly skewed distribution.
Describe the effect of an outlier on the interquartile range compared to the range.
examStyle: The heights (in cm) of 10 students are: 162, 168, 170, 165, 172, 169, 175, 164, 171, 180. Calculate the mean, median and standard deviation of these heights. [7 marks]
Compare the suitability of mean and median for summarizing exam scores that include a few very high marks. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Linear correlation and correlation coefficient
subtopics.syllabusContent: Scatter diagrams and linear correlation. Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient r. Interpretation of correlation coefficients. Use of technology.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand correlation as a measure of linear association strength and direction, distinguish between correlation and causation, and recognize limitations with non-linear relationships or outliers. Interpretation should consider context.
coreConcepts: Correlation measures the strength and direction of linear relationships between two variables
Pearson's r ranges from −1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive), with 0 indicating no linear association
Scatter diagrams visualize patterns that correlation coefficients quantify
Correlation does not imply causation; confounding variables may explain associations
Outliers and non-linear relationships can distort correlation coefficients
commonMisconceptions: Assuming r = 0 means no relationship exists (could be non-linear)
Confusing correlation with causation
Thinking higher absolute r always means better prediction regardless of context
Incorrectly calculating r by hand or misinterpreting its significance
Applying correlation to qualitative or ordinal data inappropriately

conceptual: Explain the difference between correlation and causation using an example.
Describe how an outlier can affect the value of Pearson's correlation coefficient.
examStyle: The scatter diagram shows the relationship between hours studied and test scores for 12 students. Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient r and comment on its significance. [5 marks]
Given r = 0.87 between height and weight, explain what this tells us and what it does not. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Regression and least squares line
subtopics.syllabusContent: Line of best fit (regression line) and its equation y = mx + c. Use for prediction and interpolation. Residuals and their interpretation. Use of technology.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand the least squares method as minimizing sum of squared residuals, distinguish interpolation from extrapolation, and discuss limitations of linear models.
coreConcepts: The regression line minimizes the sum of squared vertical distances from data points
Linear models enable prediction and interpolation within the range of data
Extrapolation beyond data range increases uncertainty and unreliability
Residuals measure model fit and help assess assumptions of linearity
Correlation strength influences the reliability of predictions from regression
commonMisconceptions: Using regression for causation rather than association
Extrapolating far beyond data range without justification
Confusing the regression line of y on x with x on y
Ignoring residuals when evaluating model adequacy
Assuming perfect fit when r is close to 1 without checking residuals

conceptual: Explain why the least squares regression line passes through the point (¯x, ¯y).
Describe the dangers of extrapolation when using a regression line.
examStyle: The regression line for time (x hours) and distance (y km) is y = 55.2x + 12. Find the predicted distance after 3.5 hours and comment on the reliability. [5 marks]
Calculate the equation of the regression line for the following data: x: 1,2,3,4,5; y: 3,5,4,7,8. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Probability
subtopics.syllabusContent: Sample space, events, probability of events. Rules of probability: addition and multiplication, mutually exclusive events, independent events, conditional probability.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should use tree diagrams, Venn diagrams and tables for complex probability problems, distinguish dependent from independent events, and calculate conditional probabilities.
coreConcepts: Probability quantifies uncertainty and likelihood of events in sample spaces
Addition rule applies to unions, multiplication to intersections of events
Independent events have constant conditional probabilities
Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) updates beliefs with new information
Visual tools like trees and Venn diagrams clarify complex probability structures
commonMisconceptions: Assuming independence when events are actually dependent
Adding probabilities when multiplication is required, or vice versa
Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)
Double-counting overlaps when using addition rule without subtraction
Ignoring the requirement P(B) > 0 in conditional probability

conceptual: Explain the difference between independent events and mutually exclusive events.
Describe how a tree diagram helps visualize conditional probabilities.
examStyle: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find P(second is red | first is blue). [4 marks]
Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A ∪ B). [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Discrete random variables and expectation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discrete random variables, probability mass function, expectation (mean), variance. Use of discrete probability distributions including binomial distribution.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should work with probability tables, calculate expected values and variances, and apply binomial distribution to appropriate contexts with n trials and success probability p.
