coreConcepts: Discrete random variables take countable values with associated probabilities summing to 1
Expected value E(X) gives long-run average value of repeated trials
Variance Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² measures spread around the mean
Binomial distribution models fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials
Parameters np and np(1−p) give mean and variance of binomial random variables
commonMisconceptions: Confusing expected value with most likely outcome
Incorrectly calculating variance using average squared deviations instead of E(X²) − μ²
Applying binomial distribution when trials are dependent or success probability changes
Thinking variance is always positive without considering degenerate cases
Misinterpreting probability mass function as cumulative distribution

conceptual: Explain why the expected value of a discrete random variable is a weighted average of its possible values.
Describe the conditions required for a situation to be modeled by a binomial distribution.
examStyle: A discrete random variable X has probability distribution: P(X=1)=0.2, P(X=2)=0.5, P(X=3)=0.3. Find E(X) and Var(X). [6 marks]
In 10 independent trials with success probability 0.4, find the mean and variance of the number of successes. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Bivariate discrete random variables (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Joint, marginal, conditional probability distributions for bivariate discrete random variables. Independence, expectation and covariance.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should work with joint probability tables, compute marginal and conditional distributions, and understand covariance as E(XY) − E(X)E(Y), linking to correlation.
coreConcepts: Joint distributions describe probabilities for pairs of discrete random variables
Marginal distributions are obtained by summing joint probabilities over one variable
Independence holds when joint = product of marginals
Covariance measures linear association between variables; zero for uncorrelated pairs
Correlation coefficient is standardized covariance
commonMisconceptions: Confusing joint probability P(X=x,Y=y) with conditional P(X=x|Y=y)
Summing over the wrong index when finding marginal distributions
Assuming zero covariance implies independence (true for bivariate normal but not generally)
Incorrectly normalizing conditional distributions
Thinking covariance has the same scale as variance

conceptual: Explain how to obtain the marginal distribution of X from a joint distribution table.
Describe the relationship between covariance, correlation and independence.
examStyle: The joint distribution of X and Y is given by the table... Find the marginal distribution of X, E(X), and Cov(X,Y). [8 marks]
Show that X and Y are independent given their joint probabilities. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Continuous random variables and distributions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Continuous random variables, probability density functions (pdfs), cumulative distribution functions (cdfs). Expectation, median and variance. Uniform distribution.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand pdfs integrate to 1 over their domain, use cdfs for probabilities, and calculate expectations using ∫ x f(x) dx. Uniform distribution on [a,b] has pdf 1/(b−a).
coreConcepts: Continuous random variables take uncountable values with pdfs describing density
Probabilities are areas under pdf curves; cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x)
Expected value for continuous variables uses integral weighted by pdf
Uniform distribution models equal likelihood across an interval
Median satisfies F(median) = 0.5
commonMisconceptions: Thinking pdf f(x) gives probability at x (actually density)
Confusing pdf with cdf or probability mass function
Incorrectly integrating over wrong limits for expectations
Assuming uniform distribution applies to discrete equal intervals
Forgetting pdf must be non-negative and integrate to 1

conceptual: Explain why the probability at a single point is zero for a continuous random variable.
Describe how to find the median from a continuous cumulative distribution function.
examStyle: X ~ Uniform[0,4]. Find the pdf f(x), E(X), and P(1 < X < 3). [6 marks]
Verify that f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is a valid pdf and find Var(X). [7 marks]

subtopics.title: The normal distribution
subtopics.syllabusContent: The normal distribution N(μ, σ²), standard normal distribution N(0,1). Use of tables, calculator or software. Standardization and z-scores.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should standardize to z-scores, use tables or technology for probabilities, and interpret areas under the curve. Applications to real data and quality control emphasized.
coreConcepts: Normal distribution models symmetric bell-shaped data common in nature
Standard normal allows universal tables via z = (x − μ)/σ
Probabilities correspond to areas under the density curve
68-95-99.7 rule gives approximate coverage for 1, 2, 3 standard deviations
Central Limit Theorem justifies normality for sample means
commonMisconceptions: Thinking normal distribution is the only possible continuous distribution
Incorrectly standardizing by using σ instead of σ
Reading z-table values as cumulative from right tail instead of left
Applying normal approximation without checking np and n(1−p) ≥ 5
Confusing population parameters with sample statistics

conceptual: Explain the role of standardization in using normal distribution tables.
Describe when the normal distribution provides a good model for real data.
examStyle: IQ scores are N(100,15²). Find P(85 < IQ < 115) and the 90th percentile. [6 marks]
Standardize X = 72 where X ~ N(65, 4²) and find P(X > 72) using a table. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Further probability distributions (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Poisson distribution as approximation to binomial and model for counts. Expectations and variances. Normal approximation to binomial and Poisson distributions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should know Poisson(λ) has P(X=k) = e^{-λ} λ^k / k!, E(X)=λ, Var(X)=λ. Use continuity correction for normal approximations.
coreConcepts: Poisson models rare events or counts in fixed intervals
Poisson approximates binomial when n large, p small, λ = np fixed
Normal approximates binomial/Poisson when mean large (≥10)
Continuity correction improves discrete-to-continuous approximations
Matching mean and variance guides distribution selection
commonMisconceptions: Using Poisson when events are not independent or rate varies
Forgetting continuity correction in normal approximations
Confusing Poisson parameter λ with binomial p
Applying approximations without checking conditions
Miscalculating Poisson probabilities without factorials or exponentials

conceptual: Explain the conditions under which Poisson approximates binomial.
Describe the continuity correction and when it is used.
examStyle: Typos occur at Poisson rate λ=2 per page. Find P(exactly 3 typos) and P(at most 2). [6 marks]
Approximate Bin(50,0.06) using normal with continuity correction to find P(X ≤ 4). [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Expected value and variance of discrete random variables
subtopics.syllabusContent: Properties of expectation and variance: linearity of expectation, variance of sum of independent random variables. Applications to binomial, Poisson and sums.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should prove and use E(aX+bY+c) = aE(X)+bE(Y)+c and Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X) for independent X,Y. Extend to distribution parameters.
coreConcepts: Expectation is linear regardless of dependence between variables
Variance of independent sum is sum of variances
These properties derive sums of random variables and distribution parameters
Simplifies calculations for linear combinations in probability models
Key for understanding Central Limit Theorem behavior
commonMisconceptions: Thinking Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) always (requires independence)
Incorrectly applying linearity when constants are mishandled
Confusing properties for dependent vs independent cases
Misapplying to non-linear functions of random variables
Forgetting Var(constant) = 0

conceptual: Explain why E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y) even if X and Y are dependent.
Describe how to find Var(X + Y) when X and Y are independent.
examStyle: If X ~ Bin(10,0.3) and Y ~ Bin(5,0.3) independent, find E(X+Y) and Var(X+Y). [4 marks]
Prove that Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Hypothesis testing (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Hypothesis testing for means and proportions using normal, binomial and Poisson distributions. Significance levels, p-values, Type I and Type II errors.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should set up null and alternative hypotheses, calculate test statistics and p-values, interpret results in context, and discuss errors and power.
coreConcepts: Hypothesis testing assesses evidence against a null hypothesis using sample data
p-value is probability of more extreme results assuming null true
Small p-value (less than α) rejects null in favor of alternative
Type I error rejects true null; Type II fails to reject false null
Power = 1 − Type II error probability measures test sensitivity
commonMisconceptions: Confusing p-value with P(H_0 true)
Rejecting null when p > α
Thinking small sample always gives unreliable test
Ignoring direction of alternative hypothesis (one- vs two-tailed)
Misinterpreting 'fail to reject' as 'accept null'

conceptual: Explain the difference between Type I and Type II errors.
Describe what a p-value represents and how it is used in decision making.
examStyle: Test whether the mean weight μ = 65 kg at 5% significance given ¯x=67.2, s=4.1, n=25. [8 marks]
A coin may be biased. Test H_0: p=0.5 vs H_1: p>0.5 given 28 heads in 50 tosses. Find p-value. [7 marks]

topics.title: Calculus
topics.syllabusDescription: This topic develops fundamental concepts of limits, differentiation and integration, with applications to rates of change, optimization, kinematics, areas and volumes.

subtopics.title: Limits and convergence
subtopics.syllabusContent: Informal treatment of limits, including limits at infinity. One-sided limits. Limit notation and interpretation. Convergence of sequences.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should use tables, graphs and algebraic manipulation to investigate limits. Emphasis on understanding ε-δ informally through technology and examples. Infinite limits and limits at infinity introduced.
coreConcepts: Limits describe function behavior as x approaches a value, independent of f(a)
One-sided limits capture behavior from left and right; both must agree for two-sided limit
Limits at infinity model asymptotic behavior; horizontal asymptotes
Sequences converge if terms approach a limit as n → ∞
Technology reveals limit behavior when algebraic methods fail
commonMisconceptions: Substituting x = a directly into f(x) when limit does not exist or is discontinuous
Confusing limit as x → a with f(a)
Assuming one-sided limits always agree
Thinking lim x→∞ f(x) = 0 always for rational functions
Misinterpreting non-convergent sequences as having undefined limits

conceptual: Explain why lim_{x→a} f(x) can exist even if f(a) is undefined.
Describe the difference between left-hand and right-hand limits.
examStyle: Evaluate lim_{x→0} (sin x)/x and explain its significance. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Derivatives
subtopics.syllabusContent: Derivative as rate of change and tangent slope. Limit definition of derivative. Derivatives of polynomial, rational, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should derive basic rules from first principles where appropriate, know standard derivatives, and use product, quotient and chain rules. Notation f'(x), f''(x), dy/dx.
coreConcepts: Derivative f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h gives instantaneous rate of change
Geometrically, derivative is slope of tangent line to curve
Differentiation rules enable computation for composite functions
Higher derivatives describe concavity and acceleration
Chain rule handles composition: d/dx [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) g'(x)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing average rate of change (secant) with instantaneous (tangent)
Incorrect chain rule application (forgetting inner derivative)
Misapplying product/quotient rules
Thinking derivative of sum is sum of derivatives only (actually true, but confusing)
Forgetting product rule for powers: d/dx [x^n] = n x^{n-1}

conceptual: Explain the geometric significance of the derivative function.
Describe how the chain rule is derived from the limit definition.
examStyle: Find dy/dx for y = sin(3x^2) using the chain rule. [3 marks]
Differentiate f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x^2 - 3) from first principles. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Applications of differentiation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Tangents and normals. Increasing and decreasing functions. Stationary points. Optimization problems. Kinematic problems (velocity, acceleration).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should use first and second derivative tests for maxima/minima/inflection, solve practical optimization, and interpret s(t), v(t)=s'(t), a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t).
coreConcepts: f'(x) > 0 implies increasing; f'(x) < 0 decreasing on interval
Stationary points where f'(x)=0 or undefined; classify using first/second derivatives
Optimization: critical points, endpoints; second derivative confirms nature
Kinematics: position s(t), velocity v(t)=ds/dt, acceleration a(t)=dv/dt
Normal perpendicular to tangent: slope = -1/(dy/dx)
commonMisconceptions: f'(x)>0 everywhere implies global maximum (check endpoints)
Confusing local max/min with global
Second derivative test inconclusive when f''(c)=0
Forgetting units in kinematic problems
Assuming stationary point always extremum (could be inflection)

conceptual: Explain how the first and second derivative tests distinguish between maxima and minima.
Describe the relationship between position, velocity and acceleration functions.
examStyle: Find stationary points of f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2 and determine their nature. [6 marks]
A box with square base and no lid has surface area 24 m². Find maximum volume. [8 marks]

subtopics.title: Higher derivatives and concavity
subtopics.syllabusContent: Concave up/down, points of inflection. Interpretation of f''(x). Higher derivatives f'''(x), f^{(4)}(x).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: f''(x) > 0 concave up (holds water), f''(x) < 0 concave down. Inflection where f'' changes sign. Applications to curve sketching.
coreConcepts: Second derivative f''(x) measures concavity: positive convex up, negative convex down
Inflection points where concavity changes (f'' changes sign)
Higher derivatives describe higher-order behavior and rates
Sign chart of f'' determines intervals of concavity
Concavity aids curve sketching with f, f', f'' information
commonMisconceptions: Confusing concave up with local minimum
f''(c)=0 implies inflection (must change sign)
Ignoring concavity in curve sketches
Misinterpreting higher derivatives geometrically
Assuming f'' > 0 always means increasing (no, f' determines monotonicity)

conceptual: Explain the geometric meaning of a point of inflection.
Describe how f''(x) determines the concavity of a graph.
examStyle: Find intervals of concavity and inflection points for f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3. [5 marks]
Sketch y = e^{-x} sin x using derivatives up to third order. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Implicit differentiation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Implicit differentiation of equations not expressible as y = f(x). Related rates of change. Tangents to implicit curves.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x treating y as function of x: dy/dx terms. Applications to geometry, optimization, related rates.
coreConcepts: Implicit functions define y implicitly as function of x; differentiate both sides
dy/dx obtained by chain rule on y terms
Related rates: differentiate constraint equations w.r.t. time
Combines with substitution for optimization under constraints
Essential for curves like ellipses, circles not solved for y
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting chain rule dy/dx on y terms
Differentiating constants as variables
Solving for dy/dx incorrectly after differentiation
Ignoring units/time in related rates
Assuming explicit form always possible

conceptual: Explain why implicit differentiation is needed for equations like x^2 + y^2 = 1.
Describe how to set up a related rates problem.
examStyle: Find dy/dx for x^2 + xy + y^2 = 4. [4 marks]
A ladder 10m long leans against a wall. Base moves away at 2 m/s when 6m from wall. Find rate wall distance changes. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Differential equations
subtopics.syllabusContent: First-order separable differential equations. Direction fields. Euler method for numerical solution. Geometric and algebraic interpretation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Solve dy/dx = f(x)g(y) by separation. Sketch slope fields. Euler's method: iterative approximation y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n).
coreConcepts: Differential equation relates function to derivatives modeling rates
Separable: write dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, integrate both sides
Direction fields visualize solutions through slopes at points
Euler method approximates solutions via tangent line steps
Exact solutions when separable; numerical otherwise
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting +C after integration
Incorrect separation (mixing x,y terms)
Thinking Euler always accurate (step size matters)
Confusing particular solution with general
Ignoring initial conditions until end

conceptual: Explain how a direction field helps understand qualitative solution behavior.
Describe the Euler method and its geometric interpretation.
examStyle: Solve dy/dx = xy, y(0)=1. [4 marks]
Use Euler's method with 3 steps h=0.2 to approximate y(0.6) for dy/dx = x + y, y(0)=1. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Antidifferentiation
subtopics.syllabusContent: Antiderivative (indefinite integral). Integration rules mirroring differentiation. Integration by substitution.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Reverse chain/product/quotient rules. ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C. Definite integrals later.
coreConcepts: Antiderivative F satisfies F' = f; indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C
Integration by substitution reverses chain rule: let u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx
Fundamental theorem links differentiation and integration
Constants of integration account for derivative family
Standard forms: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + C (n ≠ -1)
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting +C in indefinite integrals
Wrong substitution limits in definite integrals
Thinking ∫ 1/x dx = ln x (absolute value needed)
Confusing du with dx in substitution
Integration by parts confused with substitution

conceptual: Explain why indefinite integrals include +C.
Describe integration by substitution geometrically.
examStyle: Find ∫ (3x^2 + 2x - 1) dx. [2 marks]
∫ x e^{x^2} dx by substitution. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Definite integration
subtopics.syllabusContent: Definite integral as limit of Riemann sums and area under curve. Fundamental theorem of calculus. Areas between curves.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Net signed area; absolute area requires splitting. Trapezoidal rule approximation.
coreConcepts: Definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx = lim ∑ f(x_i) Δx (Riemann sum)
Fundamental theorem: if F' = f continuous, ∫_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)
Positive f gives area above x-axis; negative below (net signed)
Area between curves: ∫ |f - g| or split where they cross
Trapezoidal rule approximates integral via trapezoid areas
commonMisconceptions: Omitting absolute value for areas below x-axis
Wrong order b - a vs a - b
Confusing Riemann sum partitions
Thinking FTC applies to discontinuous f
Incorrect limits after substitution

conceptual: Explain the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Describe how to find the area between two curves.
examStyle: Evaluate ∫_0^{π/2} sin x dx. [2 marks]
Find area between y = x^2 and y = 2x. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Applications of integration
subtopics.syllabusContent: Volumes of revolution. Kinematic applications. Average value. Approximation methods (trapezoidal, midpoint rules).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Disk/washer/shell methods for volumes. Average = (1/(b-a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx. Numerical integration rules with error estimates.
coreConcepts: Volumes by revolution: π ∫ [R(x)]^2 dx (disks), washers similar
Average value theorem: average = integral / length
Trapezoidal rule: (h/2)(f(a)+2∑ f + f(b))
Kinematics: distance = ∫ v(t) dt, v = ∫ a(t) dt
Numerical methods approximate when antiderivative unknown
commonMisconceptions: Wrong π factor or squaring in volumes
Confusing radius with height in washers
Average as arithmetic mean vs integral mean
Trapezoidal error underestimated
Forgetting π in volume of revolution

conceptual: Explain the disk method for volume of revolution.
Describe how the trapezoidal rule approximates integrals.
examStyle: Find volume revolving y=√x from 0 to 4 about x-axis. [5 marks]
Approximate ∫_0^1 e^{x^2} dx using trapezoidal rule n=4. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Integration by parts
subtopics.syllabusContent: Integration by parts ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du. Reduction formulae. Recursive applications.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Choose u decreasing derivatives, dv easy integral. LIATE order guide. Reduction for sin^n x, etc.
coreConcepts: Parts formula from product rule: d(uv) = u dv + v du
Repeated application or substitution solves products like x e^x
Reduction formulae lower powers: I_n = ... in terms of I_{n-2}
Tabular method for multiple integrations
Choose u to simplify after differentiation
commonMisconceptions: Wrong u/dv choice leading to more complex integral
Sign errors in uv - ∫ v du
Forgetting boundaries in definite parts
Infinite loop without reduction
Confusing with substitution

conceptual: Explain how integration by parts derives from the product rule.
Describe strategy for choosing u and dv.
examStyle: ∫ x sin x dx by parts. [4 marks]
Derive reduction formula for ∫ sin^n x dx. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Series expansions
subtopics.syllabusContent: Maclaurin series for basic functions. Taylor series around other points. Binomial expansion for (1+x)^n. Remainder estimation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Series for sin x, cos x, e^x, ln(1+x), (1+x)^n. Alternating series estimation. Lagrange remainder.
coreConcepts: Taylor/Maclaurin approximate functions by polynomials matching derivatives at point
Remainder bounds convergence and accuracy
Series enable approximation, analysis near singularities
commonMisconceptions: Wrong general term factorial denominators
Infinite radius of convergence always
Confusing Taylor around a with Maclaurin (a=0)
Binomial only integers (works rationals)
Ignoring remainder for accuracy

conceptual: Explain why Taylor series approximate smooth functions well near expansion point.
Describe binomial expansion for non-integer exponents.
examStyle: Find Maclaurin series for e^x up to x^3 term. [3 marks]
Expand (1+x)^{-1/2} to 4 terms; approximate (1.02)^{-1/2}. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Differential equations (further) (HL)
subtopics.syllabusContent: Homogeneous first-order linear DEs. Integrating factor method. Second-order linear DEs with constant coefficients (basic solutions).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x): multiplying factor e^{∫ P dx}. Characteristic equation for y'' + a y' + b y = 0.
coreConcepts: Linear first-order: standard form dy/dx + P y = Q; integrating factor μ = e^{∫ P dx}
Homogeneous linear second-order: solutions e^{rt} from r^2 + a r + b = 0
Distinct real, repeated, complex roots give different forms
General solution: linear combination of fundamental solutions
Initial conditions determine constants
commonMisconceptions: Wrong integrating factor (forget dx or sign)
Confusing homogeneous DE with homogeneous solution
Characteristic roots wrong quadratic formula
Complex roots forgetting sin/cos
Particular solution neglected

conceptual: Explain how the integrating factor makes linear first-order DE exact.
Describe solution forms for different characteristic roots.
examStyle: Solve dy/dx + 2y = e^{-x}, y(0)=1 using integrating factor. [6 marks]
Solve y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Kinematic problems
subtopics.syllabusContent: Applications of differentiation and integration to motion in one and two dimensions. Velocity as derivative of displacement, acceleration as second derivative.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Variable acceleration problems using v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt = v dv/ds. Areas under v-t graphs give displacement. Kinematic equations for constant acceleration revisited via calculus.
coreConcepts: Calculus formalizes kinematics: v(t) = s'(t), a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t)
Displacement = ∫ v(t) dt, v(t) = ∫ a(t) dt + v_0
Areas under v-t: positive above t-axis (forward), negative backward
Chain rule a = v dv/ds for problems with a(s)
Solves variable acceleration beyond constant a cases
commonMisconceptions: Confusing signs: positive v forward regardless of direction change
Areas under a-t give velocity change, not displacement
Using constant acceleration formulas inappropriately
dv/ds vs ds/dt confusion
Ignoring initial conditions in integration

conceptual: Explain how the area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement.
Describe the relationship a = v dv/ds geometrically.
examStyle: Particle motion: v(t) = 3t^2 - 6t + 2 m/s. Find displacement s(3) if s(0)=0. [5 marks]
Acceleration a = 4/v where v in m/s. If v=2 when s=0, find v when s=8. [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Optimization in context
subtopics.syllabusContent: Related rates of change. Optimization problems in applied contexts including maximum/minimum volumes, costs, profits.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Implicit differentiation for related rates (ladders, expanding circles, etc.). Practical optimization with realistic constraints and multiple variables reduced via substitution.
coreConcepts: Related rates: differentiate constraint w.r.t. time, solve system
Optimization: express single variable, derivative =0, second derivative test
Real constraints: domain restrictions, physical feasibility
Economic: marginal cost = dC/dq, profit π = R - C maximized when MR = MC
Multiple critical points require comparison
commonMisconceptions: Wrong variable differentiated in related rates
Ignoring time derivatives for rates
Optimizing without domain (endpoints matter)
Absolute vs relative extrema confusion
Linear approximation near optimum

conceptual: Explain how to set up a related rates problem involving changing dimensions.
Describe the process for maximizing profit given revenue and cost functions.
examStyle: Circular pool radius increases 0.2 m/min. Find rate surface area increases when r=5m. [6 marks]
Manufacturer: C(q)=q^2/100 + 5000, R(q)=10q. Find q maximizing profit. [8 marks]
